feedback: If the learner offers more examples or a neater drawing, ask: 'How many would it take before you were CERTAIN? Is there any number that would make it a proof?'
If the learner converts to twelfths, revoice their chain back: 'so 3/4 is 9/12, 2/3 is 8/12, 9 is more than 8 - and that holds whatever you drew.'
Name success as locating a reason that covers every case at once, not as getting the right verdict.

If the learner senses the drawing isn't enough but stalls, scaffold: 'you're right it's not settled - what could you turn both fractions into so they're easy to compare?' and let them complete the chain.
activities.intendedInsight: A confirming example or a careful drawing can persuade, but a reason that holds independent of any picture is what actually settles a general claim.
learnerActions: State a claim, e.g. 3/4 > 2/3, and offer your first justification however you like (a drawing is fine to start).

When challenged ('your drawing looks close - how do I know you didn't just draw it that way? Convince me without the picture'), reach for a general reason: convert to a common denominator - 3/4 = 9/12, 2/3 = 8/12, and 9/12 > 8/12.
State explicitly why this reason settles it for ANY representation, not just your drawing.
Respond to repeated pressing ('but ALWAYS?') and refuse to let 'I tried it and it worked' count as proof.
Try the same argument on a fresh pair, e.g. 5/8 versus 2/3, to test whether your method generalises (work out the common-denominator comparison rather than guessing).
activities.title: Convince the skeptic without a picture

feedback: If the learner only says 'the total's wrong', redirect: 'which step caused it, and what did the misalignment do to the place value of that partial product?'
Confirm success when the learner links the misaligned column to the partial product sitting in the wrong place value.

A column/grid layout makes the misaligned partial product easier to locate; nudging a partial product in and out of column alignment can make the place-value cost felt (optional illustration, not required).
activities.intendedInsight: A valid critique names the flawed step and explains the underlying place-value error, which is deeper than noticing answer-disagreement.
learnerActions: Examine a worked long multiplication in which one partial product has been shoved one column to the right of where it belongs (misaligned).
Identify WHICH step is wrong, not just that the final total is off.

Explain the place-value consequence: the partial product for the next higher-place digit should sit one column further LEFT than the previous partial product (or, equivalently, end in a placeholder zero). Shoved one column to the right, it lands in a place value that is too low, so it is added into the wrong columns and contributes only one tenth of its true value.
State what the correct alignment should be and why that fixes the value.
activities.title: Find the broken step in a long multiplication

feedback: If the learner holds 'bigger denominator wins', have them test it on 1/4 versus 1/3 (equal numerators, larger denominator) and watch it fail; if they hold 'bigger numerator wins', have them test it on 3/8 versus 1/2 (differing numerators) and watch that fail - match the test case to the rule they actually hold.
Reinforce the connectives: ask the learner to join their true statements with 'because' and 'therefore' so the argument reads as a chain, not a list.

Distinguish an incorrect comparison rule (a false belief about fraction size) from a reasoning gap; if the learner misranks fractions, revisit comparison via a common denominator or a benchmark before judging their reasoning.
activities.intendedInsight: One counter-example is enough to refute a general claim, whereas confirming examples alone never establish one - and each step of an argument should be linked by because/therefore.
learnerActions: Consider a claim such as 'the fraction with the bigger denominator is always bigger' or 'the fraction with the bigger numerator is always bigger'.
Test the bigger-denominator claim where the numerator is held fixed: compare 1/4 and 1/3 - the denominator 4 is larger, yet 1/4 is smaller than 1/3, so that claim fails.

Test the bigger-numerator claim on a case where the numerators actually differ: compare 3/8 and 1/2 - the numerator 3 is larger than 1, yet 3/8 is smaller than 1/2 (since 1/2 = 4/8), so that claim fails too.
State each breaking case as a counter-example that disproves the rule.
Articulate the asymmetry: one counter-example disproves a general claim, but any number of confirming examples does not prove it.
Build a because/therefore chain linking the givens to the conclusion so a list of true facts becomes a connected argument.
activities.title: Counter-examples and the asymmetry of proof
